title: Joshua 12:7–24
context: The list continues west of the Jordan with the thirty-one kings Joshua and Israel defeated, from Baal Gad near Mount Hermon to Mount Halak toward Seir. Many of the cities appear in the campaigns of chapters 6–11, including Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron, Lachish, and Hazor. Others are mentioned here for the first time or only rarely. Some are widely identified, such as Jericho, Lachish, Megiddo, and Hazor; others are uncertain, and a few names differ in ancient versions. Defeating a king did not always mean the city was permanently held. Jerusalem remained in Jebusite hands until David (Joshua 15:63; 2 Samuel 5:6–9), and Gezer was not driven out (Joshua 16:10). Both traditions read the list as a record of God keeping his promise, while honestly noting that possession of the land was gradual.

verses.text: These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the children of Israel struck beyond the Jordan westward, from Baal Gad in the valley of Lebanon even to Mount Halak, that goes up to Seir. Joshua gave it to the tribes of Israel for a possession according to their divisions;
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the kings Joshua and Israel defeated west of the Jordan, from Baal Gad to Mount Halak, and Joshua gave the land to the tribes. The western list begins.

Arminian readers note that the land given to the tribes would require faithful settlement and obedience in each generation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the same boundaries as in 11:17 frame the list, emphasizing the completeness of God’s gift.

Both traditions read the verse as a summary of God keeping his promise through Joshua, preparing for the allotments in chapters 13–19.

verses.text: in the hill country, and in the lowland, and in the Arabah, and in the slopes, and in the wilderness, and in the South; the Hittite, the Amorite, and the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite:
verses.arminianNotes:
The land includes hill country, lowland, Arabah, slopes, wilderness, and the South, home of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. The variety of terrain and peoples is noted.

Arminian readers note that the list of peoples echoes God’s earlier promises, showing that his word was being fulfilled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the six peoples named here correspond to lists in Exodus and Deuteronomy, a reminder that God’s promise was specific.

Both traditions see the verse as connecting the list of kings with the promise of land.

verses.text: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Jericho and the king of Ai beside Bethel are listed, one each. These are the first two victories in the land (Joshua 6–8).

Arminian readers note that Jericho shows victory through faith, while Ai shows defeat through disobedience before victory came.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Jericho fell by God’s direct act and Ai only after Achan’s sin was dealt with. God’s holiness governs victory.

Both traditions draw from these two cities lessons about faith, obedience, and the seriousness of sin among God’s people.

verses.text: the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Jerusalem and the king of Hebron are listed. Both joined the southern coalition defeated in Joshua 10.

Arminian readers note that although Jerusalem’s king was defeated, the city itself was not taken until David (2 Samuel 5:6–9; Joshua 15:63).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Jerusalem would later become the city God chose for his name, and Hebron the place where David first reigned. God’s purposes for these cities reached far beyond this list.

Both traditions read the verse as part of a long story of promise.

verses.text: the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Jarmuth and the king of Lachish are listed. Both were part of the southern coalition (Joshua 10:3).

Arminian readers note that these kings chose to join an alliance against Gibeon, Israel’s new ally, and so came under judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Lachish is widely identified with a large site in the Shephelah, and it appears again in later history. God’s dealings with these cities span centuries.

Both traditions treat identifications cautiously and read the verse as testimony to God’s faithfulness in the southern campaign.

verses.text: the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Eglon and the king of Gezer are listed. Gezer’s king came to help Lachish and was defeated (Joshua 10:33).

Arminian readers note that Gezer itself was not driven out (Joshua 16:10), showing that defeating a king did not always mean possessing a city.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Gezer later came into Israel’s hands as a gift to Solomon (1 Kings 9:16). God’s purposes for the land unfolded over generations.

Both traditions see in Gezer a reminder that fulfillment can be gradual and surprising.

verses.text: the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Debir and the king of Geder are listed. Debir was taken in the southern campaign (Joshua 10:38–39).

Arminian readers note that Debir appears again when Othniel captures it (Joshua 15:15–17), a sign that some cities had to be retaken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Geder is not otherwise known, and its location is uncertain. God’s record includes places history has largely forgotten.

Both traditions hold the details cautiously and read the verse as part of the cumulative witness to God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Hormah and the king of Arad are listed. Both are connected with events in Numbers 21:1–3.

Arminian readers note that Israel’s victory at Hormah followed a vow made in prayer, showing the people’s dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Judges 1:17 also connects Hormah with Judah and Simeon, which interpreters harmonize in different ways.

Both traditions read the verse as linking the wilderness generation’s experience with the conquest under Joshua.

verses.text: the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Libnah and the king of Adullam are listed. Libnah was taken in Joshua 10:29–30.

Arminian readers note that Adullam later became the place where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1), and where many in distress gathered to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s providence prepared places that would serve his purposes long after the conquest.

Both traditions take encouragement that God’s care for his people reaches across generations, even through the names of ordinary towns.

verses.text: the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Makkedah and the king of Bethel are listed. At Makkedah five kings hid in a cave (Joshua 10:16–28).

Arminian readers note that Bethel, where Jacob met God (Genesis 28:19), is also listed, and was later taken by the house of Joseph (Judges 1:22–26).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Bethel’s name recalls God’s covenant promise to Jacob, now being fulfilled. Later, Bethel became a center of false worship (1 Kings 12:28–29).

Both traditions see in Bethel both promise and warning.

verses.text: the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Tappuah and the king of Hepher are listed. Little is known about these cities.

Arminian readers note that the list includes places otherwise unrecorded, a reminder that faithful obedience often goes unnoticed by history.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s record of victory is complete, including cities whose locations are now uncertain. Nothing escaped his notice.

Both traditions avoid speculating on locations and read the verse as part of the full account of God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lassharon, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Aphek and the king of Lassharon are listed. Several places were named Aphek, and Lassharon is uncertain; some ancient versions read the names differently.

Arminian readers note the textual question and hold it with patience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that such uncertainties are part of honest study of an ancient text, and they do not affect the passage’s meaning.

Both traditions read the verse as part of the list of kings God delivered into Israel’s hand, without building anything on the uncertain names.

verses.text: the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Madon and the king of Hazor are listed. Both appear in the northern coalition of chapter 11.

Arminian readers note that these kings chose to join Jabin’s alliance, and their defeat followed that choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Hazor, once the head of all those kingdoms, is now one name among many. God brings down the proud.

Both traditions read the verse as connecting the list to the narrative of the northern campaign, showing the completeness of God’s victory.

verses.text: the king of Shimron Meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Shimron Meron and the king of Achshaph are listed. Both were among the kings Jabin summoned (11:1).

Arminian readers note that the list carefully records each king who resisted, showing the responsibility each one bore.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the list confirms the narrative: every king named in the coalition was defeated. God’s word through Joshua was fulfilled.

Both traditions treat the identification of these sites cautiously and focus on the theological point.

verses.text: the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Taanach and the king of Megiddo are listed. Both cities later appear in Deborah’s song (Judges 5:19).

Arminian readers note that these cities were not immediately possessed (Judges 1:27), showing the ongoing need for faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Megiddo is widely identified and became a significant site in later history, and many interpreters connect it with the name Armageddon in Revelation 16:16.

Both traditions hold that connection cautiously while affirming God’s rule over history.

verses.text: the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Kedesh and the king of Jokneam in Carmel are listed. Several places were named Kedesh.

Arminian readers note that one Kedesh later became a city of refuge (Joshua 20:7), showing God’s provision of mercy within the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Carmel later became the scene of Elijah’s contest with the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). God’s purposes for these places reached far beyond the conquest.

Both traditions read the verse with care, without speculating on exact sites.

verses.text: the king of Dor in the height of Dor, one; the king of Goiim in Gilgal, one;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Dor in the height of Dor and the king of Goiim in Gilgal are listed. Some ancient versions read Galilee instead of Gilgal.

Arminian readers note that Dor was mentioned in 11:2 and that the textual question about Goiim does not affect the passage’s meaning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Goiim means nations, and that the reading of the place name is uncertain. Scholars propose different identifications.

Both traditions hold these questions with humility and read the verse as part of the record of God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: the king of Tirzah, one: all the kings thirty-one.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Tirzah is listed, and the total is thirty-one kings. The list closes with a count.

Arminian readers note that the number records the extent of God’s faithfulness while Israel’s task of possession was still ahead.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Tirzah later became a capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 15:33). The count stands as a memorial of God’s victories.

Both traditions read the closing total as an invitation to remember and give thanks for what God had done, while trusting him for what remained.
